intro: The idée fixe makes its last appearance as a grotesque dance, then disappears. Bells introduce another kind of memory: the Dies irae chant from the Mass for the Dead. Berlioz eventually combines that borrowed melody with the witches’ round. Follow the Dies irae thread to distinguish this actual chant quotation from later composers’ very different uses of its text and tune.
question: What happens when a love melody and a funeral chant become dance music?

sections.label: The idée fixe disfigured
sections.mNote: The beloved’s melody becomes a grotesque dance

sections.label: Bells and expectation
sections.mNote: The dance withdraws before the funeral chant

sections.label: Dies irae
sections.mNote: A borrowed funeral chant changes register and rhythmic scale

sections.label: Witches’ round
sections.mNote: A new dance tune passes between imitating voices

sections.label: Towards the combination
sections.mNote: The final region prepares and combines chant with dance

sections.label: Headlong close
sections.mNote: The combined nightmare drives towards its final chords

cues.title: A gathering without a tune
cues.text: The opening offers tremors, short calls and separated gestures before any sustained melody takes charge. Berlioz’s programme imagines a grotesque gathering for the artist’s funeral. Listen to the scattered sounds as preparation for a scene, not as a tune you have failed to recognise.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 1–20, and programme, movement V. Report shows low levels and multiple changes within the first minute; the dramatic interpretation comes from the programme.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The gaps matter
cues.text: Notice how reduced sound makes each new gesture conspicuous. The introduction does not build in one straight line. Its hesitations give the coming dance a sharper edge than an uninterrupted crescendo would provide.
cues.evidence: Report: quiet windows at 0:35–0:40 and 1:20–1:25 separate stronger gestures; structural changes include 0:36, 0:46 and 1:06.

cues.title: A nightmare after the scaffold
cues.text: This scene follows the artist’s imagined execution. The programme does not resurrect the beloved as a consoling figure: she joins the sabbath. The same melody that once represented longing is about to acquire a deliberately degrading dramatic role.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s programme, movements IV and V, describes the execution dream and the beloved’s arrival at the sabbath.

cues.title: The beloved’s distorted dance
cues.text: Listen for the idée fixe reshaped into a quick, ornamented dance. The score moves from an initial clarinet glimpse to the sharper E♭ clarinet colour. The melody remains recognisable, but its rhythm and delivery deny the dignity of its first appearance.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 21–78, including the E♭ clarinet statement; programme calls the melody vulgar and grotesque. Report: changes around 1:34–1:50 lead into a lighter, active passage at 1:50–2:20. Instrument identities are score-based.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An abrupt dismissal
cues.text: The transformed melody does not remain the finale’s principal subject. A forceful burst and subsequent withdrawal clear the ground for different material. Keep the idée fixe in memory, but do not expect it to organise the rest of the movement as it organised the first.
cues.evidence: Score commentary: the idée fixe is dismissed after bars 21–78. Report: the strong 2:35–2:45 region gives way to much quieter windows from 3:00.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The funeral becomes audible
cues.text: Berlioz specifies deep funeral bells, part of the nightmare’s ceremonial setting. The written notes are C and G. Their role is not to carry the whole tune, but to frame the arrival of a melody associated with the Mass for the Dead.
cues.evidence: Score, bell part from bar 102; programme names funeral bells before the Dies irae. No claim is made about the particular bells used in this session.

cues.title: The Dies irae chant
cues.text: The broad, low melody in this region quotes the Dies irae chant. Its opening turns down, back up, then lower. Follow that small contour: it will remain identifiable when Berlioz shortens the note values and changes the orchestral colour around it.
cues.evidence: Score labels the chant Dies irae from bar 127, initially in bassoons and ophicleides. Report: the near-silence at 3:40 is followed by a strong, low-brightness passage at 3:45–4:00. This locates the region approximately.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A chant made less solemn
cues.text: Berlioz changes the chant’s rhythmic scale and scoring. Listen for the same melodic outline becoming shorter and more mobile rather than for a completely new tune. The parody depends on recognition: a funeral melody is being made to participate in the dance.
cues.evidence: Score, Dies irae episode, bars 127–221, shows successive rhythmic diminutions and changes of instrumental group. Report supports the contrasting active region after the broad low statement; no individual handover is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Prepare a second memory
cues.text: You now have one melody to retain: the funeral chant. A different tune will organise the witches’ round. Keep them separate at first, because the finale’s later combination is easier to hear when each has already acquired a distinct shape.
cues.evidence: Score and programme distinguish the Dies irae from the Ronde du Sabbat and later combine them. This cue prepares the comparison without claiming an exact new-theme entrance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A round built by imitation
cues.text: The witches’ round passes its tune between voices, with new entries joining before earlier ones have finished. Listen for overlap rather than a succession of solo turns. Learned contrapuntal technique helps build the nightmare’s increasingly crowded dance.
cues.evidence: Score, Ronde du Sabbat from bar 241, begins in lower strings and adds imitating entries. Approximate placement follows the score sequence and the report’s active middle span; no individual entry is synchronised.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Layers rather than one mass
cues.text: Try following one repeated contour through the changing orchestral weight. When several lines overlap, the loudest part is not necessarily the only important one. The round’s construction becomes clearer if you listen for entrances and continuations separately.
cues.evidence: Score, extended imitative Ronde du Sabbat, bars 241–347. This is a listening strategy for the passage, not instrument recognition from the audio report.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A programme that changed
cues.text: In the 1845 programme Berlioz treated the written scenario as indispensable. In the revised 1855 preface he allowed the symphony to be performed on its own without that explanation. The music’s recurring shapes can therefore be followed without turning every sound into an illustrated object.
cues.evidence: The two programme versions and their prefaces are reproduced on the Hector Berlioz Website, Symphonie fantastique: Texts and Documents.

cues.title: Withdrawing before the collision
cues.text: The busy middle region retreats to a quieter, darker texture. Listen through the reduction rather than treating it as exhaustion. It prepares the final span in which previously separate ideas are brought into a shared orchestral space.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level falls towards −34.6 dB at 8:00 and −37.7 dB at 8:10; brightness is much lower than in the preceding active passages.

cues.title: Pressure returns from below
cues.text: A restrained texture gathers force again. Follow the accumulating activity across the swell: the finale is preparing more than a louder repeat. Its two established musical worlds are moving towards a confrontation.
cues.evidence: Report: −36.6 dB at 8:15 rises to −5.6 dB at 8:50, with increased detected attacks around 8:25–8:30. The larger formal interpretation comes from the score.

cues.title: Chant and round together
cues.text: In the final region, listen for the broad chant against the quicker dance. These are not two episodes placed side by side: Berlioz superimposes familiar material. Try following the slower contour while allowing the faster figures to continue around it.
cues.evidence: Score and programme explicitly combine Dies irae and Ronde du Sabbat in the concluding region. Report: the renewed strong passage around 9:00–9:25 follows the preceding build. Timing is passage-level, not a claim that the combination starts at 9:20.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Wood against strings
cues.text: One late change of colour comes from col legno: violins and violas strike their strings with the wood of the bow. Listen for the dry, percussive quality amid the dance. A familiar string section can become a source of noise as well as sustained melody.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 444–460, marks col legno for violins and violas. Report: a lighter, attack-rich region around 9:40–10:00 supports approximate placement, including 6.0 detected attacks per second at 9:55; the technique itself is score evidence.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: No return to consolation
cues.text: The ending drives towards forceful final chords rather than recovering the first movement’s devotional calm. Listen to how much of the orchestra has become part of the rhythmic machinery. The nightmare closes by intensifying its energy, not by restoring the beloved’s original melody.
cues.evidence: Score, concluding coda; report: sustained strong levels from 10:25 to 10:55, with the loudest window at 10:55, followed by a sharp decay.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two kinds of recurrence
cues.text: The symphony has transformed its own idée fixe and borrowed an older chant. Those are different relationships: one binds the five movements together; the other brings a shared musical association into the finale. The Dies irae thread traces what other composers make of that inherited material.
cues.evidence: Programme and score establish the cyclic idée fixe and the quoted Dies irae. The linked influence thread supplies the wider comparison; no further event is claimed during the recording’s final decay.

transitions.title: A remembered melody changes character
transitions.how: The fragmented introduction gives way to the last appearance of the idée fixe. A tentative clarinet glimpse and orchestral interruption lead towards its sharper, dance-like transformation. The familiar outline survives while its pace and colour change.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 21–78; report changes at 1:34 and 1:38, followed by the active lighter region from 1:50. The boundary marks the approach, not an exact E♭ clarinet entrance.

transitions.title: The dance withdraws
transitions.how: The beloved’s grotesque dance is dismissed. A darker, more exposed passage prepares the bells and funeral material. This is a change of dramatic subject: the idée fixe will not return as the finale’s organising melody.
transitions.evidence: Score, transition after bar 78 and bells from bar 102; report changes around 2:58–3:14 and a substantial fall in brightness at 3:00–3:10.

transitions.title: The funeral chant takes shape
transitions.how: After the bell-framed preparation, a broad low melody becomes the focus. Its deliberate pacing makes the chant easy to retain before Berlioz alters its rhythmic scale and orchestral colour.
transitions.evidence: Score, Dies irae at bar 127; report boundary at 3:46 and level jump after the very quiet 3:40 window, with low brightness at 3:45–4:00.

transitions.title: A second tune joins the nightmare
transitions.how: The chant episode gives way to the witches’ round, whose tune is developed through imitating entries. Keep its quicker profile distinct from the chant’s opening: the final combination depends on having heard the two materials separately.
transitions.evidence: Score, end of Dies irae episode at bar 221 and Ronde du Sabbat from bar 241. The report’s more active region around 5:25–5:45 provides a broad location, not a demonstrated first-entry second.

transitions.title: Separate ideas approach one another
transitions.how: The round’s busy texture thins before another build-up. The closing region will bring the chant and dance together rather than merely alternating them. Listen for the preparation as well as the eventual superimposition.
transitions.evidence: Score commentary groups bars 348–524 as the approach to and realisation of the final combination. Report shows a trough at 8:10–8:15 followed by a build to 8:50.

transitions.title: The final drive takes over
transitions.how: The late contrasts of articulation and orchestral colour feed a final sustained drive. The ending concentrates the movement’s energy instead of recovering the intimate voice of the idée fixe.
transitions.evidence: Score, final coda after the late col legno episode; report grows stronger from around 10:10 and sustains high levels through 10:55. Approximate listening division.

source.title: Berlioz, Songe d’une nuit du Sabbat — orchestral score
source.locator: Bars 1–20, 21–78, 102–223, 127–221, 241–347 and 348–524. Stage “tuba” represents the score’s ophicleide parts; no historical instrument identification is claimed for this recording. Bells share the percussion group.

facts: Flute and guitar as a boy; Paris Conservatoire with Jean-François Le Sueur and Anton Reicha
Critic for the Journal des débats; Conservatoire librarian; touring conductor
Shakespeare, Goethe and Virgil supplied the subjects of his largest works
Four symphonies; operas; dramatic and sacred choral works; songs; an orchestration treatise
composer.background:
Berlioz grew up in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, in the household of a physician who taught him Latin and expected him to study medicine. He learned flute and guitar, but never acquired the pianist’s routine of composing at a keyboard. Virgil’s account of Dido’s death affected him as a schoolboy; forty years later he would set it in Les Troyens. Sent to Paris in 1821, he attended anatomy lectures while spending his evenings at the Opéra. The theatre’s performances of Gluck offered a different education: declamation, orchestral gesture and the pacing of a dramatic scene.

He abandoned medicine, studied with Jean-François Le Sueur and entered the Conservatoire in 1826. His first large works included a Messe solennelle and the unfinished opera Les Francs-juges, whose overture survived independently. The Prix de Rome required a prescribed cantata; Berlioz finally won it in 1830, on his fourth attempt. The prize sent him to the Villa Medici, but the decisive musical experiences had already happened in Paris. Conservatoire performances under François-Antoine Habeneck introduced him to Beethoven’s symphonies, while an English theatrical company introduced him to Shakespeare.
composer.epithet: He made orchestral colour, the position of a sound in space, and the return of a remembered melody into structural events.
